---
title: "Recipes: one block of bytes, many readings"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

`bin_unpack()` and `bin_decode()` never consume their input: the same bytes can be read at
the same offset as many ways as you like, which is what a C `union` does. Each recipe here is
a few lines over bytes written out in full, so that it runs as it stands.

```{r setup}
library(zubin)
bits <- function(v, from, width) (v %/% 2^from) %% 2^width
```

`bits()` takes `width` bits starting at bit `from` of a whole number, for fields narrower
than a byte; zubin's fields are whole bytes.

## A market data feed: Nasdaq TotalView-ITCH

ITCH 5.0, Nasdaq's order-book feed, is a stream of messages of different sizes. Each message
opens with a one-letter type that decides the layout of the rest, and in the files Nasdaq
publishes each one is framed by its length as a big-endian `u16`. A few of the message
types, as the specification lays them out:

```{r itch-layouts}
common <- ">type:s1 locate:u16 tracking:u16 ts_hi:u16 ts_lo:u32"
itch <- list(
  A = bin_layout(paste(common, "ref:u64 side:s1 shares:u32 stock:s8 price:u32")),
  E = bin_layout(paste(common, "ref:u64 shares:u32 match:u64")),
  D = bin_layout(paste(common, "ref:u64"))
)
vapply(itch, bin_size, numeric(1))
```

`A` adds an order, `E` executes part of one and `D` deletes it. The timestamp is a 6-byte
count of nanoseconds since midnight, a width no machine type has, so it is two fields that
add up: `ts_hi * 2^32 + ts_lo`. Prices are fixed-point with four decimals.

A file of five messages, framed as Nasdaq frames them:

```{r itch-feed}
frame <- function(type, ...) {
  body <- bin_pack(itch[[type]], type = type, locate = 1, tracking = 0, ...)
  c(bin_encode(length(body), "u16", endian = "big"), body)
}
t0 <- 9.5 * 3600 * 1e9 # 09:30, in nanoseconds
ts <- function(s) list(ts_hi = (t0 + s * 1e9) %/% 2^32, ts_lo = (t0 + s * 1e9) %% 2^32)
feed <- c(
  do.call(frame, c("A", ts(0), ref = 1, side = "B", shares = 100, stock = "ZUBN    ", price = 123400)),
  do.call(frame, c("A", ts(1), ref = 2, side = "S", shares = 50, stock = "ZUBN    ", price = 123500)),
  do.call(frame, c("E", ts(2), ref = 1, shares = 40, match = 1)),
  do.call(frame, c("D", ts(3), ref = 1)),
  do.call(frame, c("E", ts(4), ref = 2, shares = 50, match = 2))
)
length(feed)
```

Reading it takes two passes. The first walks the frames, which only needs each length, and
records where each message starts and its type:

```{r itch-walk}
starts <- numeric(0)
at <- 0
while (at < length(feed)) {
  len <- bin_decode(feed, "u16", offset = at, n = 1, endian = "big")
  starts <- c(starts, at + 2)
  at <- at + 2 + len
}
types <- vapply(starts, function(s) rawToChar(feed[s + 1]), "")
types
```

The second reads all the messages of one type in one call. They are scattered through the
file, so they are gathered first into a run of records of their own:

```{r itch-read}
gather <- function(x, starts, size) x[as.vector(outer(seq_len(size), starts, "+"))]

read_type <- function(type) {
  l <- itch[[type]]
  m <- bin_unpack(gather(feed, starts[types == type], bin_size(l)), l)
  m$time <- format(.POSIXct((m$ts_hi * 2^32 + m$ts_lo) / 1e9, tz = "UTC"), "%H:%M:%OS3")
  m[setdiff(names(m), c("locate", "tracking", "ts_hi", "ts_lo"))]
}

adds <- read_type("A")
adds$stock <- trimws(adds$stock)
adds$price <- adds$price / 1e4
adds
read_type("E")
```

For a day's file of a few hundred million messages the walk in R is the slow part; the reads
are one call per message type whatever the count.

## One identifier, three views: a UUID

A UUID is 16 bytes, read as a `u128`, as the five groups of its text form, or by the bits
that say which kind of UUID it is:

```{r uuid}
id <- as.raw(c(0x55, 0x0e, 0x84, 0x00, 0xe2, 0x9b, 0x41, 0xd4,
               0xa7, 0x16, 0x44, 0x66, 0x55, 0x44, 0x00, 0x00))

g <- bin_unpack(id, ">a:b4 b:b2 c:b2 d:b2 e:b6", as = "list")
paste(vapply(g, function(f) paste(f[[1]], collapse = ""), ""), collapse = "-")

v <- bin_unpack(id, ">x6 version:u8 x1 variant:u8 x7")
c(version = bits(v$version, 4, 4), variant = bits(v$variant, 6, 2))
```

Version 4 is a random UUID, and variant `2` (`10` in binary) is the RFC 9562 layout.

## One address, two views: IPv6

The 16 bytes of `2001:db8::1` are eight 16-bit groups, or a 32-bit prefix (`2001:db8::/32`,
the range set aside for documentation) followed by the rest:

```{r ipv6}
ip <- as.raw(c(0x20, 0x01, 0x0d, 0xb8, rep(0, 10), 0x00, 0x01))
groups <- unlist(bin_unpack(ip, ">g:u16[8]"))
sprintf("%x", groups)
bin_unpack(ip, ">prefix:u32 host:b12")$prefix == 0x20010db8
```

## A Windows timestamp: one `u64`, or two `u32`

A `FILETIME` counts 100-nanosecond intervals since 1601-01-01 in a `u64`, and the Windows
headers declare it as two `u32`, low word first. Today's count is past 2^53, so read as a
double it would be rounded, and zubin refuses rather than round:

```{r filetime, error = TRUE}
ft <- as.raw(c(0x00, 0xe0, 0xfb, 0x31, 0xaf, 0x63, 0xdd, 0x01))
bin_decode(ft, "u64")
```

As an `integer64` it is exact, and whole seconds come out by integer division. bit64's
methods need its namespace loaded; attaching it is not necessary:

```{r filetime-64}
invisible(requireNamespace("bit64", quietly = TRUE))
ticks <- bin_decode(ft, "u64", int64 = "integer64")
ticks
.POSIXct(as.numeric(ticks %/% 10000000L) - 11644473600, tz = "UTC")
```

The two words are each exact as doubles. Their sum is not, past 2^53, but it is within 16
ticks, 1.6 microseconds, which is far below a second:

```{r filetime-words}
w <- bin_unpack(ft, "<low:u32 high:u32")
w
.POSIXct((w$high * 2^32 + w$low) / 1e7 - 11644473600, tz = "UTC")
```

## A pixel: one `u16`, three channels

RGB565, the pixel format of many small displays, packs red, green and blue into 5, 6 and 5
bits of a little-endian `u16`. Read as integers, the channels come out with `bits()`:

```{r rgb565}
px <- bin_decode(as.raw(c(0x00, 0xf8, 0xe0, 0x07, 0x1f, 0x00, 0xff, 0xff)), "u16")
data.frame(word = sprintf("%04x", px),
           red = bits(px, 11, 5), green = bits(px, 5, 6), blue = bits(px, 0, 5))
```

## R's missing values under another type

R's `NA` for doubles is a NaN whose low word holds 1954; its `NA` for integers is the smallest
32-bit integer, which as an unsigned integer is 2^31:

```{r na}
bin_unpack(bin_encode(NA_real_, "f64"), "<low:u32 high:u32")
bin_decode(bin_encode(NA_integer_, "i32", na = "allow"), "u32") == 2^31
```

`NaN` differs from `NA` only in that low word, which is how `is.na()` and `is.nan()` tell
them apart:

```{r nan}
bin_unpack(bin_encode(c(NA, NaN), "f64"), "<low:u32 high:u32")
```

## The same bytes, either byte order

A format whose byte order you are not sure of can be read both ways, and the plausible
reading kept. A TIFF file opens with `II` (little-endian) or `MM` (big-endian) and then 42 in
that order:

```{r tiff}
tiff <- as.raw(c(0x4d, 0x4d, 0x00, 0x2a, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0x08))
order <- if (rawToChar(tiff[1:2]) == "II") "<" else ">"
bin_unpack(tiff, paste0(order, "order:s2 magic:u16 first_ifd:u32"))
bin_unpack(tiff, "<order:s2 magic:u16 first_ifd:u32")
```

The first reading is the right one; read little-endian, the same magic number is 10752.

## In other languages

The same problems motivate binary-data libraries elsewhere, and their examples are worth
reading next to these:

| Library | Language | Its leading example | Here |
|---|---|---|---|
| [`struct`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/struct.html) | Python | format strings over bytes | the layout string |
| [construct](https://github.com/construct/construct) | Python | a BMP-like header: magic, width, height, pixels | the README's PNG header |
| [`encoding/binary`](https://pkg.go.dev/encoding/binary) | Go | a `float64`, a small struct, varints | `bin_decode()`, `bin_unpack()` |
| [binary-parser](https://github.com/keichi/binary-parser) | JavaScript | an IPv4 header; TLV records through `choice` | the ITCH feed |
| [restructure](https://github.com/foliojs/restructure) | JavaScript | records with pointers, versions and bitfields | the ITCH feed, RGB565 |
| [deku](https://github.com/sharksforarms/deku) | Rust | an RGB565 pixel | RGB565 |
| [binrw](https://github.com/jam1garner/binrw) | Rust | a record with a magic number, a count and a counted array | the ITCH frames |
| [nom](https://github.com/rust-bakery/nom) | Rust | parser combinators, from a hex colour to FLV, pcap and TLS | — |
| [Kaitai Struct](https://kaitai.io/) | many | declarative specifications of hundreds of real formats | — |

Most of them go further than zubin in one direction: following offsets stored in the data,
counts and choices inside one declaration, or varints. zubin keeps a layout to one fixed-size
record and leaves the walk between records to R, as the ITCH recipe does, so that each read
is one call over every record.
